title: Sacromonte Lead Book 17, Haqiqat al-Injil ('Libro mudo', the 'mute book'): five or six lead plates in an undeciphered cryptic script
correspondents: unknown (attributed by its editors to the Morisco forgers of the Lead Books, probably Miguel de Luna)
language: unknown (Arabic expected: the Lead Books are in Arabic, and the plate-1 seal legend in Arabic calls the text 'maqlubat al-'allama', an inverted sign)
shelfmark: Abadía del Sacromonte, Granada, archive: Libros plúmbeos, Lead Book 17 (lp17), Haqiqat al-Injil, 16 lead plates; Vatican Library photographs iii, 1-16 (the books were in Rome until 2000)
folio_note: 16 plates: plates 2-6 (7?) carry 9-10 lines each of cryptic script, numbered 1-7 in dots; plate 1a is a Seal of Solomon with an Arabic legend (read, a six-line poem); the rest are blank or drawings. Only fol. 3b is published as a photograph (van Koningsveld and Wiegers 2024, fig. 14, p. 114; 10 lines). Sibling: one line of the same kind of cryptic script in lp16, fol. 6a (fig. 29, p. 332; fig. 35).
status: Undeciphered according to its 2024 critical editors ('a cryptic script ... that has baffled all scholars who have worked with these materials, including the experts of the seventeenth-century Vatican Commission', p. 113; edition entry p. 348: 'an undeciphered cryptic script'). They incline to pseudo-cryptography because the script has many more signs than the Arabic alphabet (p. 115). Contemporary accounts call it 'el libro mudo' because most of it could not be read (p. 57); Miguel de Luna interpreted only the seal poem. Not on DECODE (searches Sacromonte, Granada, plomo, lead book: 0); not in the repository (known.py: Sacromonte, Libro mudo, plúmbeos, Lead Books: no hits).
why: The 'mute book' is the text the Lead Books present as their central message, held back for the End of Time; a reading, or proof that it is meaningless, bears on how the Morisco forgers of 1595-1599 built the whole affair.
score_note: Scored after viewing the one published plate (fig. 14 of the 2024 edition, 1,313 x 1,317 px) during the Arabic sweep 2 part A (research/sweep_2026-11-16_arabic_2/part_A.md)
verify: Ask the Abadía del Sacromonte (or the Vatican Library, photographs iii, 1-16) for images of plates 2-7; check Hagerty, Los libros plúmbeos del Sacromonte (1980) and Barrios Aguilera (2011) for any transcription of the signs; count the sign inventory on fol. 3b and compare with the magical alphabets of Ibn Wahshiyya and al-Jildaki (the editors' suggested family).

seen.extent: fol. 3b: 10 ruled lines across the whole plate, with a two-sign heading; the edition says plates 2-6 (7?) each carry 9-10 such lines, about 50 lines in all
seen.cipher: Engraved angular signs on ruled lines, run in word-like groups with dot clusters above and below many signs; not Arabic letters, though some shapes recall Kufic forms. Nothing on the plate glosses it, and the edition prints no reading of any cipher plate: only the Arabic seal legend on fol. 1a is read. At this size single signs and dots are distinct; a lead plate carries no interlinear writing.

vetting.key_check: No key is known. The editors compare the script with the magical alphabets of Ibn Wahshiyya (Shawq al-mustaham) and al-Jildaki, without a match, and note that it has more signs than the Arabic alphabet; neither alphabet was tested here. The Colin 1927 Saadian key is a different system (28 signs in abjad order) and was not tested.

title: Gordon (Khartoum) to Mustafa Pasha Yawar, Mudir of Dongola: Arabic note largely in two-digit numeral cipher, found among Dongola papers in 1886 and sent to Grenfell for a key
correspondents: Charles George Gordon (signature 'Ghurdun', with 'bi-khatmihi' for his seal) -> Mustafa Pasha Yawar, Mudir of Dongola
shelfmark: Durham University Library, Archives and Special Collections, Sudan Archive, Wingate papers, SAD.250/1/550 (with the covering letters SAD.250/1/549 and 549v)
folio_note: One leaf, canvas 35 of 96 of the digitised unit SAD.250/1/528-606 (native 2,107 x 3,264 px). Address line in clear ('li-sa'adat Mustafa Basha Yawar mudir Dunqula'); then 15 lines of about 8 Eastern Arabic two-digit numbers each (about 120 numerals), with a few Arabic words left in clear among them and a few numbers corrected above the line; then 3 lines mostly in clear Arabic with a few numerals; date and signature. No decipherment on the leaf.
status: Durham catalogue: 'E. Palmer and Grenfell re a note written in code by Gordon (SAD.250/1/549-550)'. On the image: Palmer to Grenfell, 15 Nov 1886: among papers received from Dongola he found 'a scrap of paper containing figures signed by Gordon. He evidently had a code', one of Grenfell's Sudan employees (name read as Khalil Ibrahim, uncertain) has the key; 'The figures are in Arabic'. Grenfell's reply on 549v: 'I have the key. If you will send ... the papers I will translate & send back to you.' No translation is filed with it (folios 543-548 and 551-556 viewed at 500 px: field-day orders and the Emin Bey report). Not on DECODE (decode_search.py: Gordon, Dongola, Durham University, Sudan Archive: 0). known.py: SAD.250 appears only as a catalogue-only side line in research/sweep_2026-11-15_arabic part C and D; not in leads.json or catalogue.json. Gordon's Journals (Hake 1885) print two other notes from Gordon to the Mudir of Dongola (15 Shawwal 1301 and 7 Dhu'l-hijja 1301), both in clear, not this one. TNA PRO 30/57/4/26 (Kitchener papers, Gordon Expedition telegrams, [1884]) is described as a 'translation from Arabic script cipher respecting repayment of a loan' (see also PRO 30/57/3/11): not opened (TNA catalogue page 403 to this session); it could be the decode of this or a sibling note.
why: A surviving original of Gordon's Arabic numeral cipher from the siege of Khartoum, addressed to the Mudir of Dongola; it would show the system his scribes used (which, by Slatin's letter printed in the Journals, the Mahdists broke) and add a Gordon message of early November 1884.
score_note: Scored from the image during the 16 Nov 2026 Arabic sweep 2, part B (research/sweep_2026-11-16_arabic_2/part_B.md)
verify: Ask TNA for PRO 30/57/4/26 and PRO 30/57/3/11 (Kitchener papers) and compare with this note; search FO 407 (Confidential Print) Nov-Dec 1884 and the Kitchener/Wingate printed collections for a translation of a Gordon note to the Mudir of Dongola of 16 Muharram 1302; read the date line and the clear words with an Arabist; the numerals (a small set, about 25 distinct values, with clear words mixed in) look like a letter or syllable substitution that the clear words and the address may unlock. Vetting block withheld: the possible contemporary translation at TNA (PRO 30/57/4/26, 3/11) and FO 407/63 (Nov-Dec 1884, read only by OCR grep) are unanswered; the date line and the ratio of clear words should be checked by an Arabist.

why: An owner's or reader's private note in cipher in an 18th-century copy of a popular romance; it would add one more Ottoman-period Arabic private cipher, of the kind otherwise known mainly from treatises.
